Regarding Visas, I have been travelling here for many years on a tourist visa whilst working in Hong Kong, and just recently converted it to a visa by marriage. comments.author: @abritincambodia
comments.text:
These AI-generated videos concern me a little when they present figures without giving the full picture.

I've lived in the Philippines for over 11 years and was blogging there for most of that time. I've only been out of the Philippines for seven months, and I'm now living and blogging in Cambodia, so I still have a very good understanding of what life is actually like for ordinary people there.

I know many Filipino workers who are earning nowhere near ₱19,630 a month. I personally know people working for major companies who are earning around ₱14,000 a month.

So I would be very careful about presenting ₱19,630 as though that is the average wage for Filipino workers. It certainly isn't representative of what many ordinary workers are actually earning, even in Manila.

There is also a big difference between what the official figures say and what people actually experience. Workers can be expected to stay late or work additional hours, and when you're on a relatively low wage and need your job, refusing isn't always as straightforward as it sounds.

I've spent 11 years living and blogging in the Philippines, and I've now made the move to Cambodia and continued blogging here. I honestly think moving to Cambodia was one of the best decisions I've ever made.

If anyone is interested in what life is really like from the perspective of a British expat who has actually lived in both countries, I've been documenting it all through my blogs: A Brit in the Philippines and A Brit in Cambodia.

I'm certainly not claiming to know everything, but after 11+ years living and blogging in the Philippines and now living in Cambodia, I think I have a pretty good idea of what I'm talking about.

comments.author: @oldguyinmanila
comments.text: The current Jeepneys are built for people under 5'6" and will fill your lungs full of the smoke from all the jeepneys ahead of you. If you don't want to end up sick with congestion, don't do it. Beer at an outdoor spot still costs the same as beer in the grocery store in the U.S. and none of the places serving it at these prices can compare with your patio back home--a filthy toilet or none at all, just a wall or a bush to pee on. But the price of a liter of a fifth of Gilbey's Gin is just $4. The size of the apartment prices he quotes is 240 square feet, the size of a 30 foot motorhome. If you get a comparable size apartment to the US apartments, it's 1/2 to 2/3 the price of a US apartment. BUT the cost of air-conditioning is double what it runs in most cities, so tack on an extra hundred to that half price. BUT, the security in the tiny condo where I live is astounding. Turnstiles to enter, guards everywhere, if you have a visitor the guard knocks on your door before allowing them through the front lobby, a grocery store underneath the building I live in? Yep, including a mall. So I'm at $450 with electricity included for my motorhome sized, 1 bedroom unit. Eating what working Filipinos eat means eating 80% starch to 20% meat. I wouldn't take chances eating at karenderias, so if you're eating outside of your residence, you'll be paying $7-$12 for a meal at a chain restaurant (clean food) that serves to your table. High end all inclusive buffets in the mall cost around $13-$20. Doctors are VERY cheap but you better make sure you have plenty of cash/credit to get out of the hospital once you're ready to be released because they won't let you leave until you pay. Your body will be impounded in the hospital, for days, weeks, or however long it takes you to come up with the payment for the hospital's total cost. Surgery and hospitalization that takes a couple of days of hospitalization up to a week costs around $3000, at least that's what it cost for emergency gallbladder removal for a relative of mine. The cost of actually residing in the Philippines is much cheaper than the cost to travel because beef is $3 - $5 per pound, eggs and chicken are about the same price as the US. Milk is non-existent or unrecognizable. Imported butter from New Zealand is lower than US prices. Cheese, forget it. It's all imported and all very expensive.

The minimum wage in the Philippines ranges from ₱350 to ₱755 per day, depending on the region and the specific industry.There is no single national rate. Instead, regional boards set daily pay rates based on local living costs.
Regional Daily RatesNational Capital Region (Metro Manila): ₱755 for non-agriculture workers and ₱718 for agriculture and small businesses (rising to ₱780 and ₱743 in January 2027).
Central Luzon (Region III): ₱475 to ₱600.
CALABARZON (Region IV-A): ₱485 to ₱600.
Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR): ₱505.
Caraga (Region XIII): ₱350 to ₱475

replies.author: @100DOLLARCAMERA
replies.text:
Micro-Enterprises & Small Retail: Establishments regularly employing 15 or fewer workers, as well as micro-manufacturing businesses, follow a lower baseline tier: ₱658 per day (rising to ₱718 per day under NCR-27).  
 Income Tax Exemption: Statutory Minimum Wage Earners (SMWEs) in the Philippines are 100% exempt from paying personal income tax on their basic daily wage, holiday pay, night differential, and overtime pay.
 Mandatory Deductions: Employers must still deduct employee contributions for SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG, while providing the legally mandated 13th-month pay by December.
